findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will usually be cancelled
findings.body: Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) derive the legacy timeout context from ctx, which is the incoming request context embedded with the logger. The Kubernetes API handler cancels that context when the request returns, and Mode 3 returns immediately after spawning the goroutine. The legacy operation therefore races request completion and will often receive context.Canceled before writing, silently defeating the stated safety copy to legacy storage. The goroutine should derive from a detached context (for example context.WithoutCancel or a background context, preserving needed values) before applying the 10-second timeout.

findings.title: Async Update reuses the same UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the object already written to unified storage
findings.body: Storage.Update has already consumed objInfo to compute the updated object from the unified-storage version. The goroutine then passes the same objInfo to Legacy.Update, which will fetch the legacy (different) old object and call UpdatedObject again. That second computation can carry the unified-storage ResourceVersion/UID state and fail optimistic-concurrency or validation against legacy, or produce different content than what was committed to unified storage. The previous implementation wrapped objInfo in updateWrapper carrying the exact object returned by Storage.Update; dropping that wrapper is a regression for the dual-write update path.

findings.title: Async Create passes the storage-mutated input object to legacy Create
findings.body: d.Storage.Create(ctx, obj, ...) is commonly implemented by mutating the passed-in obj in place (setting ResourceVersion, UID, creation timestamp, generated name). The goroutine then passes that same obj to d.Legacy.Create. Legacy create can therefore see a non-empty ResourceVersion/UID and reject the create, or create a legacy record whose identity/RV does not match a fresh create. Legacy should receive a copy cleared/derived from the returned created object (as other dual-writer modes do by stripping ResourceVersion), and doing the copy after Storage.Create also needs to happen before the caller can mutate the returned object.

findings.title: Storage failures and DeleteCollection legacy result are recorded against the wrong metric
findings.body: On Storage.Create failure (line 45) and Storage.Update failure (line 129) the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ..., startStorage) even though legacy was never attempted, so storage errors pollute the legacy latency/error series and no storage error is recorded. In DeleteCollection the async legacy call at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency is counted as storage latency. Delete success at line 106 also passes `name` in place of the kind used by every other call, creating inconsistent/high-cardinality metric labels. This makes the mode-3 dashboards/alerts used to judge migration safety wrong.

findings.title: Legacy async failures are never logged and a legacy panic crashes the process
findings.body: All four async legacy goroutines only record a duration metric: the returned error is never logged (and in Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection there is not even a log line naming the object on failure), and there is no recover. Because mode 3 promises legacy is written 'just as a safe measure', an operator cannot discover from logs that the safety copy is failing, and a panic in Legacy storage code inside the detached goroutine is not recovered by the HTTP handler middleware and will crash the server process.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes and share one mock for both stores
findings.body: The tests construct legacyStoreMock and storageMock around the same *mock.Mock, so a call to either store satisfies indistinguishable expectations, and they never call AssertExpectations / AssertCalled for the legacy Create, Update or Delete paths (Delete/DeleteCollection tests do not even register legacy expectations). Because the legacy calls now run in unsynchronized goroutines, the tests pass even if legacy is never written, and if the goroutine fires after the test finishes it can race with subsequent tests reusing the package-level example objects/mock state. The async behaviour (legacy called, with what object, within the timeout) is the core feature of mode 3 and needs synchronised assertions (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup in the mock).

findings.title: New mode 3 integration cases immediately assert legacy visibility and are racy
findings.body: The new file/unified mode 3 subtests reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates/updates/deletes via the k8s API and then immediately checks the legacy API (getFromBothAPIs and the legacy list/search checks). Under the new implementation the legacy write is fire-and-forget with a 10-second window, so there is no happens-before guarantee when those legacy assertions run; the test will be flaky and can also pass spuriously if a later assertion happens to be late enough. The mode 3 integration case needs polling/eventual-consistency assertions for the legacy side (or to wait for the async write) rather than the synchronous checks used for modes 1/2.
